paras: The killing of William Lewis was the fatal shooting of a Black man, also called Billy Lewis, by L. W. Jamison, a horse trainer, at Jamison's house on the fair-grounds in Springfield, Illinois, on the evening of August 6, 1880. Jamison said he fired on Lewis for attempting to assault a young servant girl, and the first wire reports carried that account under headlines such as "A Would-Be Outrager Shot." After Lewis died the next day, a coroner's inquest heard that the assault story was a "pretense" and that he had been killed to conceal Jamison's relations with the girl, and Jamison and the girl were committed for murder.

Jamison lived on the Springfield fair-grounds with his wife and a 20-year-old girl, Hattie Carpenter, who lived in the family; wire versions named her Hattie White and called her his servant. He was from Kentucky and had "some reputation as a trainer of running horses." Lewis, according to the Chicago Tribune, was really named Fawcett and had formerly lived at Franklin, Indiana.

In the version printed on August 7 in a Springfield special to the Chicago Tribune, Mrs. Jamison had gone downtown after supper when Lewis came to the house intoxicated, tried to "outrage the girl," and chased her through the house. Jamison, returning, picked up a revolver, ordered Lewis to halt, and fired three times, one ball entering his side between the ribs and hip. The Chicago wire as printed in Wilmington had Jamison hearing an outcry while tending horses, snatching a pistol from a washstand, and shooting as Lewis fled. The Tribune's correspondent noted that "several stories" circulated but judged the facts "about as stated."

Lewis died at about 6 o'clock on the evening of August 7. Before his death he made a statement that he had caught Jamison and the girl "in improper relations," that she first tried to shoot him and failed, and that Jamison then took the revolver and shot him.

Accounts differ on how Jamison came into custody: the Tribune said neighbors arrested him, while the wire said he surrendered himself. At the coroner's inquest on August 7, testimony showed a "criminal intimacy" between Jamison and Carpenter that Lewis knew of and had threatened to report, and both were committed to jail on a coroner's warrant charging murder. When the inquest resumed on August 8, witnesses said Jamison habitually carried a pistol and had threatened several neighbors, and the testimony was reported to show "deliberate murder." The jury recommended that Jamison be held without bail; no report of an indictment or trial was found in the coverage.

The story reached readers in two forms. A Chicago dispatch of August 7 spread Jamison's account east, appearing in the New-York Tribune as "Killed for Assaulting a Servant" and in the Washington Evening Star and the Wilmington Daily Gazette as "A Would-Be Outrager Shot." A one-sentence brief saying Jamison shot Lewis "for attempting to feloniously assault" the girl ran in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer on August 9 and again in the Westminster, Maryland, Democratic Advocate on August 14, after the inquest findings had been published in Chicago.

Only the Chicago Tribune, through its own Springfield correspondent, followed the case to the inquest. Its first item, headed "Brought Him Down," endorsed Jamison's account, but the next two were headed "He Was Murdered" and "Held for Murder" and called the attempted rape the "pretense for the shooting." Every report identified Lewis as "a negro" or "colored" while giving no race for Jamison, and no Black-press coverage of the killing was found.

Two accounts of the shooting conflict. Jamison's, carried by the wire, held that Lewis was shot while fleeing after an attack on the girl, while Lewis's dying statement and the inquest testimony held that he was shot after discovering Jamison and the girl together. The later Chicago reports rest on an inquest and a dying declaration, whereas the wire version came from Jamison alone. The papers also differ on the girl's surname, Carpenter or White, and the Evening Star placed the shooting on Saturday rather than Friday night.

reader.title: Killing of William Lewis (Springfield, Illinois)
bases: One man, L. W. Jamison, shot Lewis at his home on the Springfield fair-grounds, with the girl in his household accused by Lewis of first trying to shoot him; no mob, posse or officers took part (A1, A2, A4).

All reports agree Jamison shot and killed Lewis (A1, A2, A3, A7), but the wire's account of an attempted assault on the girl is contradicted by Lewis's dying statement and the coroner's inquest, which found deliberate murder (A2, A4).

framing.detail: Eastern papers ran the Aug. 7 Chicago wire as 'A Would-Be Outrager Shot' and 'Killed for Assaulting a Servant', presenting Jamison's claim as the reason for the shooting.
A one-sentence brief said Jamison shot Lewis 'for attempting to feloniously assault' the girl and carried no later correction.
The Chicago Tribune first gave Jamison's account as 'about as stated' under 'Brought Him Down', then reversed with 'He Was Murdered' and 'Held for Murder' after the inquest.

Shot after catching Jamison and the girl together; deliberate murder to silence him (dying statement, inquest)

conflicts.note: The inquest testimony and Lewis's dying statement are later and sworn or formal; the wire version rests on Jamison's account alone.
The Springfield specials to the Chicago Tribune consistently say Carpenter.
The Aug. 6 dateline of A1 supports Friday.
